title: Moringa Biotin Laddus: A Nutritionist's Take on Natural Hair Fall Remedies
excerpt: Nutritionist Kiran Kukreja shared a moringa and biotin-rich laddu recipe targeting hair health, combining traditional Indian sweets with functional nutrition.
body:
Nutritionist Kiran Kukreja has shared a recipe for moringa biotin laddus that she describes as a natural approach to combating hair fall — a common concern among Indian women both in the subcontinent and abroad. The recipe, originally published in Hindustan Times, combines moringa powder with biotin-rich nuts and seeds in the traditional Indian laddu format.

The Recipe

The moringa biotin laddu uses a base of dry-roasted seeds and nuts — including black sesame seeds, flax seeds, almonds, and pumpkin seeds — ground into a coarse powder and combined with moringa powder, desiccated coconut, and cardamom. Seedless dates provide natural sweetness and binding, while a small amount of ghee helps the mixture hold its shape.

The preparation is straightforward: dry roast the seeds and nuts on low heat until aromatic, cool and grind to a coarse powder, blend dates into a paste, then combine everything with moringa powder and ghee. The mixture is shaped into small balls while still warm. The laddus can be stored in an airtight container for 7-10 days at room temperature or up to three weeks when refrigerated.

"The Nutritional Case Moringa, often called the "drumstick tree" across South Asia, has drawn attention from nutrition researchers for its dense concentration of micronutrients."

Kukreja recommends eating one laddu daily, preferably in the morning, as part of a balanced diet rather than as a standalone treatment.

The Nutritional Case

Moringa, often called the "drumstick tree" across South Asia, has drawn attention from nutrition researchers for its dense concentration of micronutrients. The leaves contain significant amounts of iron, calcium, vitamins A and C, and various antioxidants. Iron deficiency is one of the most common nutritional causes of hair loss, particularly among women.

The other ingredients in the laddu contribute additional nutrients associated with hair health. Black sesame seeds are rich in zinc and calcium. Flax seeds provide omega-3 fatty acids that support scalp health. Almonds offer vitamin E, which has been linked to improved hair growth in some studies. Pumpkin seeds contribute zinc and protein.

Biotin — vitamin B7 — plays a role in the production of keratin, the protein that forms hair, skin, and nails. While clinical biotin deficiency is relatively rare, subclinical deficiency is more common and can contribute to hair thinning. The combination of peanuts, almonds, and sunflower seeds in the recipe provides natural biotin sources.

Expert Perspective

Dermatologists and nutritionists generally agree that diet plays a role in hair health, but caution against treating food-based remedies as medical solutions. Hair loss can result from hormonal changes, genetic factors, stress, thyroid disorders, and other medical conditions that require clinical evaluation.

Nutrient-dense foods like the ingredients in this laddu can support overall health, including hair health, but they are best understood as part of a comprehensive approach rather than a targeted treatment. Kukreja's framing of the recipe as a daily supplement, not a cure, aligns with this measured perspective.

The Laddu Wellness Trend

The recipe reflects a broader trend of adapting traditional Indian sweets into functional health foods. Laddus made with combinations of nuts, seeds, superfoods, and natural sweeteners have become popular across social media, with variations targeting everything from immunity to energy to postpartum recovery.

For the diaspora, recipes like these serve a dual purpose: they offer a familiar format that fits into daily routines, and they provide an alternative to supplement capsules by delivering nutrients through whole foods. The accessibility of the ingredients — most are available at Indian grocery stores worldwide — makes this a practical addition to any kitchen.
